name: Attar oils / alcohol-free perfume

card.summary: Concentrated alcohol-free perfume oils with a long traditional history, discussed as a grooming scent option with no appearance research behind them.
card.note: Pure oils are concentrated; skin reactions to fragrance ingredients are possible.

quick.overview:
Attar oils are traditional perfume oils made by distilling flowers, woods and other botanicals into an oil base instead of alcohol.

In grooming communities they are mentioned as an alcohol-free scent alternative. No clinical research has tested them for attractiveness or appearance.
quick.mechanism: The aromatic materials are steam- or hydro-distilled, often into sandalwood oil, then aged. The result is worn on the skin as a scent.
quick.risks: Sources reviewed do not document specific harms. As with any concentrated fragrance material, individual skin sensitivity can occur.

lead: Attar (also spelled ittar) is a perfume oil made from botanical or other natural materials, usually by hydrodistillation or steam distillation, with an oil as its base rather than alcohol.[1] It is worn on the skin as a fragrance, and in grooming and looksmaxxing discussions it appears as an alcohol-free alternative to colognes: a way to smell good, which people treat as part of how they present themselves.

Alcohol-free fragrance making is described as going back over 3,000 years in India and Egypt, with production centres in India such as Kannauj, Delhi and Mumbai.[1] No published clinical studies have examined attar oils as an appearance or attractiveness aid.

chain: Distilled botanical oil applied to the skin
Fragrance that wears close to the body
angle.text: Attar is worn as a personal fragrance. People who prefer oil-based scents use it for a signature smell that sits on the skin without the alcohol of a spray cologne.

infobox: Oil (often sandalwood oil or liquid paraffin) rather than alcohol[1]
One to ten years on a wood base[1]

paras: Traditional attar is distilled into a wood base such as sandalwood and then aged, from one to ten years depending on the botanicals and the desired result.[1] The best-known method is the deg-bhapka process, in which copper vessels, bamboo pipes, clay seals and steam carry floral essence into the oil.[1] Sandalwood oil and liquid paraffin are named as common bases.[1] Fragrances are commonly grouped as 'warm' (musk, amber, saffron), associated with winter, or 'cool' (rose, jasmine, khus), associated with summer.[1]

Rose attar is classed as a cool fragrance used in summer.[1] Musk was traditionally taken from the Siberian musk deer, whose demand has endangered several species, and synthetic 'white musk' is now common; Musk Tahara is a personal fragrance used in the Middle East and the Muslim world, now mostly made with synthetic musk.[1] Amber attar refers to ambergris, a waxy substance from sperm whales, and is classed as warm.[1]

Alcohol-free fragrance making in India and Egypt is described as more than 3,000 years old, with Indian scents travelling along the Silk Road; the Hindi-Urdu words attar and ittar are believed to have been applied once they reached the Middle East.[1] Avicenna is credited with an early rose-distillation technique, and Queen Arwa al-Sulayhi of Yemen introduced a variety made from mountain flowers.[1] Attars are used in Hindu and Buddhist household and temple offerings, and by some Sufi groups in shrines.[1]
